New units authorized less the existing homes the same projects demolish, compared with the counterfactual's own new units and demolitions on those sites. It is net authorized capacity: the change in the housing stock if every authorized project is finished. It is not observed stock growth, which needs completion and demolition events by date.
Authorizations moved into or out of the window by a timing mechanism, the rest newly feasible; observed completions and modelled deliveries kept apart from simulated permits.

Bound: how many of these a local permit system records, and how many a survey respondent reports as new construction, is unknown. Read the line as the most the reform could add outside the survey definition, not a measured count.
Unavailable: no completion series is read for this state, so no observed completion is reported.
Not modelled: no completion lag is applied, so no permit is turned into a delivered home here. The authorized net change if completed is the upper limit of what these permits could add to the stock.
No mechanism in this reform pushes a permit past 2031; a start delay lowers the total instead (permits not issued are not moved).

The survey covers places that issue building permits; a place with no permit requirement is outside it. The Census Bureau imputes figures for permit offices that did not report, and since 2023 it updates the set of permit offices every year. The baseline projects the published figures, imputations included.

Current law is the law in force on the as-of date. A rule enacted on or before the as-of date with a later effective date is current law from its effective date: when that date falls inside 2027-2031 it is modelled as a reform with a start delay equal to the years between January 1, 2027 and the effective date (the reform's start_delay_years entry), and the run names it. Bills not enacted by the as-of date are scenarios, never baseline. The benchmark reforms are assumed in force on January 1, 2027.

Interest rates, construction costs, rents, home values and household incomes are held at the levels in the ledger and the data packs for the whole window (2027-2031). The baseline repeats recent permit trends under today's rules; it does not predict a recession or a boom. Only the ranges of the ledger entries and the baseline's back-tested range carry uncertainty about them.

New privately owned housing units authorized by building permits, as the Census Bureau's Building Permits Survey counts them, in the five calendar years 2027-2031. A reform's number is the difference from the baseline in the same unit: permits the reform adds, less permits the baseline would have issued anyway on the same sites. The Building Permits Survey leaves out additions, alterations, renovations and conversions of existing buildings, so a unit created that way is not in this measure.

Added units authorized count every new unit that needs a permit. Net added homes subtract the existing homes a project demolishes (the reform's share of them: a demolition that would have happened in the baseline anyway is not the reform's). One house replaced by three homes is three authorizations and two more homes.

What these estimates cannot tell you
These are ranges of building permits, not a forecast of homes finished.
A reform's likely range is a simulation range: it shows how the result moves with the assumptions, given the baseline. No reform of this kind has past totals to check it against.
They describe the whole state. They do not say which lots, streets or owners would build.
They do not say who would live in the new homes or what they would pay.
They assume every town follows the new rule from the first day and approves permits at today's pace.
They say nothing about years after the five-year period.
The baseline repeats recent permit trends under today's rules. It does not predict a recession or a boom.

The baseline range is not a promise. Tested on past years, using only what was known at the time, ranges built this way caught the real five-year total less often than eight times in ten for counties. Each range states how often ranges like it caught the real total.
Those past years hold about one housing cycle, and misses ran mostly to one side and moved together across counties, so the share caught rests on few independent periods.

The rule behind the range was chosen using every past year, including the years it was later scored on, and with today's county types rather than those known at the time, so the share caught is somewhat favourable. Each count's validation card names the study, years and area it comes from.
Counties without a permit office, or with imputed permit counts, carry the Census Bureau's estimates.

The year between the last full year of permit data and the first projected year has no full-year count yet. The baseline carries the latest yearly level through it; a nowcast from the monthly files is shown as a check only, and a part-year count is never treated as a full year.

The middle value depends on which past years the rule averages. In Pennsylvania one unusually high year sits in the window; the baseline card shows the effect of leaving it out as a disclosed sensitivity, not a replacement.

In states with a short permit record, the range is widened toward the past errors of states that grew at a similar pace. Those errors come from one recovery after a housing bust, so the next cycle may differ, and the ranges still caught the real total less often than they aim to.

Where the baseline itself has been least accurate in past years: Philadelphia (one county, but far off: it has tended to run too low), small counties (where it has tended to run too high) and rural counties (where it has tended to run too high). CHAS is a special tabulation of the 2018-2022 survey, rounded and with margins of error; it is older than the 2020-2024 figures in other sections. Income bands are shares of HUD's area median family income for the household's HUD area. Tract figures carry no margins and are often very uncertain. Income limits and rents are for the county's HUD area. Assisted homes are counted from HUD's lists; programs overlap, only two contracts per property are dated, tax-credit records stop at 2020 projects, and tax-credit restrictions are counted as ending at year 30 (some last longer). Most expiring contracts are renewed. Nothing here predicts displacement, rent changes or the loss of any home.

Zoning must provide for housing of various dwelling types: single-family and two-family homes, a reasonable range of multifamily homes in various arrangements, and mobile homes. An ordinance is not invalid for leaving out any other specific type. A comprehensive plan must include a plan to meet the housing needs of present and expected residents, which may provide for new housing in different dwelling types at densities suited to households of all incomes. Zoning may allow more density or intensity than a district's base rule when a project meets standards written in the ordinance (a density bonus). Municipalities may adopt traditional neighborhood development rules: walkable, mixed-use neighbourhoods with a greater variety of dwelling types than lot-by-lot zoning gives. It is optional.

Municipalities other than counties may adopt an impact fee ordinance, but only for off-site road (transportation) improvements listed in a transportation capital improvements plan, charged as a condition of final plat approval. The code authorizes no other kind of impact fee. Impact fees may pay only for road improvements caused by new development; they may not pay for other municipal facilities, repair and upkeep, or fixing existing shortfalls. Before adopting a transportation impact fee, a municipality must appoint an advisory committee and prepare a transportation capital improvements plan built on land use assumptions and a roadway sufficiency analysis. Sewer and water tap-in or connection fees must be worked out as the Municipality Authorities Act provides. Subdivision and land development review fees must be reasonable and necessary and set by a fee schedule adopted by ordinance or resolution.

HB 2186 (2025-2026), Printer's No. 3373, new 53 Pa.C.S. Chapter 63. One ADU per lot, attached or detached, would be allowed by right wherever a home is a permitted use. Municipalities could not require owner occupancy, a family tie between occupants or extra parking, and could cap size no lower than 850 square feet or half the house, whichever is less. Passed the House 139-62 on June 1, 2026. Applies to: Every municipality with zoning where a residential building is permitted (cities included).

SB 1346 (2025-2026), Printer's No. 1747, new MPC § 603.2. At least one ADU per single-family detached home would be a permitted use by right in every district where such homes are permitted, approved without a hearing. Owner occupancy and extra parking could not be required; an ADU could be rented but not sold separately. Applies to: Municipalities under the Municipalities Planning Code (all but Philadelphia and Pittsburgh).

Counties and municipalities could not require a minimum number of parking spaces for any development or building, whatever its use, except spaces required by the Americans with Disabilities Act. It would take effect one year after enactment. Applies to: Every county and municipality.

Screening measures only: they show where building may be harder, not what the rules allow, and they do not change the model's estimates. The flood share uses FEMA's regulatory 1% annual chance floodplain; it leaves out heavy-rain flooding away from mapped streams, and some flood maps are decades old. A home counts as in the floodplain when its 2020 Census block's centre point falls on a 30 m grid cell inside the floodplain, so large rural blocks are coarse. Land cover is a 30 m satellite classification; developed land includes parks and lawns. Slope comes from a 30 m elevation grid, which smooths short steep banks, so the steep share is a lower bound for small sites.

American Community Survey 5-year table-based summary files (2020-2024)

Estimates are survey averages over five years with margins of error; small tracts often have wide margins. One national pipe-delimited file per table (about 48 MB for B25024). Negative values are missing-value codes, not data.
American Community Survey 5-year tables for the place-profile charts (2020-2024)

Survey estimates averaged over five years, with margins of error; tract counts in small bands are often very uncertain. Bands are sums of published cells; a band's margin is the Bureau's approximation for a sum. To keep the pack small, tracts keep only age, race and ethnicity, household income, commute mode and rent burden (counties and the state keep every table).
FHFA House Price Index, annual, counties

Repeat-sales index built from mortgages bought or guaranteed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac; thin in rural counties, where years can be missing. Published as a spreadsheet (read with the standard library's zip and XML tools).
LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES 8), workplace area characteristics, all jobs
U.S. Census Bureau, Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics program

Counts jobs covered by unemployment insurance plus federal civilian jobs, by where people work. Self-employed people, the military and informal work are not counted. A person with two jobs counts twice. The Census Bureau adds noise to block counts for privacy; tract and county sums are much steadier.
LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES 8), home-to-work flows, all jobs

Links each job's workplace block to the worker's home block. The "main" file covers jobs with both ends in the state; the "aux" file adds workers who live in another state. Residents who work in another state are in that state's files, which are not read, so out-commuting across the state line is not counted. Same job coverage as the workplace file.

Counts private establishments with paid employees and their mid-March employment and yearly payroll. Government, self-employed and most farm work are left out. Small cells carry noise; the noise flag is kept. Establishments that cannot be placed in a county are left out, so counties do not add up to the state total.
Building Permits Survey, county annual files
Counts units authorized by permit, not units started or finished. Some counties are imputed rather than reported; the file flags which. Places without permit offices are not covered.
Comprehensive Housing Affordability Strategy (CHAS) data, Tables 8, 12 and 15C
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Policy Development and Research (special tabulation of ACS data by the Census Bureau)

Survey estimates averaged over five years, rounded by the Census Bureau, with margins of error; small tract cells are very uncertain. Income bands are shares of HUD area median family income (HAMFI) for the household's area, not of a county's own median. Cost burden is housing costs (gross rent, or owner costs) over household income; households with no or negative income are "not computed". The edition is older than the ACS 2020-2024 tables used elsewhere.
HUD income limits (Section 8), area median family income and 30%, 50% and 80% limits by household size
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Policy Development and Research

Limits are set per HUD area (a metro area or a non-metro county) with caps, floors and state non-metro adjustments, so the 80% limit is not always 1.6 times the 50% limit and the 30% limit can be raised to the poverty guideline. The 60% and 100% figures used for rents are derived from the 50% limit (x1.2 and x2), the convention HUD uses for tax-credit limits; they are not published here.
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD eGIS open data)

Properties with an active HUD project-based assistance contract (Section 8, Section 202/811 and similar). Only the first two contracts of a property carry units and an expiration date; a third or later contract is not dated here. Many contracts are renewed when they expire, so "expiring" marks a renewal decision, not a certain loss. Properties that also hold tax credits are counted in both programs.

Public housing developments as reported by housing agencies; a scattered-site development is one point. Units converted to project-based contracts (RAD) leave this list and appear among assisted multifamily properties.
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit properties (HUD LIHTC database)
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development

Projects placed in service since 1987 as reported by state agencies; recent years are incomplete (the map service's Pennsylvania records stop at 2020) and the year is unknown for some projects. A project's point is the address of its largest building. Projects that left the program are not removed.
HUD Housing Choice Vouchers by Tract (map service)

Households using a tenant-based voucher, by the tract of the home they rent. Vouchers move with the household, so they are assisted households, not assisted homes, and are kept apart from the unit counts. Small counts are suppressed by HUD.
The Gap: A Shortage of Affordable Homes, 2026 (cited benchmark, not ingested)
State level only. Built by NLIHC from ACS microdata (PUMS) with its own income and affordability rules; not comparable cell by cell with CHAS. Quoted as context, never used in a calculation.
Philadelphia Licenses and Inspections building permits (permits)
City of Philadelphia, Department of Licenses and Inspections (via OpenDataPhilly, Carto SQL)

Permits issued, not homes started or finished. A record-system change in 2020 renamed permit types; both names are counted. A 2021 rush ahead of a tax abatement change inflates that year. The table has an issue date but no application date; building permits link to their zoning permit from late 2019.
City of Pittsburgh, Department of Permits, Licenses and Inspections (via WPRDC)
No home counts, so only permits are counted. City of Pittsburgh only, not the rest of Allegheny County.
PHFA Low-Income Housing Tax Credit award lists

Awards, not homes built: some awarded projects are delayed or dropped. Read from PDFs whose layout changes yearly; a list with no text layer is skipped. Sites described as intersections or scattered sites have no tract.
Municipal Statistics, County / Municipal Planning, Zoning & Building Code report
Pennsylvania Department of Community and Economic Development (DCED)

Self-reported by municipalities and updated when they tell DCED; some entries may be out of date. Says whether an ordinance or plan exists, not what it allows or when it was last revised. DCED ids are matched to Census county subdivisions by name; unmatched names are listed in the build notes.
Pennsylvania municipal zoning ordinances published on each municipality's own website

Five municipalities read by hand so far, out of about 2,560; all others are unknown. Posted copies can lag amendments. Commercial code hosts (eCode360, Municode, American Legal) are never read: their terms forbid bulk or automated use.
City of Philadelphia, L&I Accessory Dwelling Unit Checklist (PZ_004_INF, Rev 3.2022)
City of Philadelphia, Department of Licenses and Inspections
City guidance from 2022, not the Zoning Code itself (section 14-604(11) is hosted by a commercial code host and is not read); a 2026 amendment could not be checked, so the row stays draft.
City of Pittsburgh legislation (Bill 2025-1545, Ordinance 31 of 2026, accessory dwelling units)

One ordinance. The web record above is the human-readable page; the text itself was read by script from the city's Legistar web API (https://webapi.legistar.com/v1/pittsburgh/matters/31504/texts/35471, version 7, the pinned one; 31504 is the API's matter id, not the web site's). Struck and inserted words are read from the API's RTF marks. The attachment server (pittsburgh.legistar1.com) disallows robots, so no PDF is read. The full Pittsburgh Code is hosted by a commercial code host and is not read.
County comprehensive plans (citation list in assumptions/plans.yaml)

A citation list for all 67 counties with the planning commission's link; 34 plans are confirmed with name and adoption year on the county's page, the rest are marked not confirmed. Each county's own page is the authority.
Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code (Act 247 of 1968, as amended), full text

The unofficial text the General Assembly publishes; Purdon's and the official Laws of Pennsylvania are the authority. Does not reach Philadelphia or Pittsburgh. Says what municipalities may or must do, not what each one did.
Pennsylvania House Bill 2186 (accessory dwelling units), bill page and text
A proposed bill, not law, unless enacted; it lapses at the end of the session. Status is re-checked after November 30.
Pennsylvania Senate Bill 1346 (accessory dwelling units), bill page and text
A proposed bill, not law, unless enacted. Applies only to municipalities under the Municipalities Planning Code, so not to Philadelphia or Pittsburgh.
Pennsylvania House Bill 2155 (municipal parking minimums), bill page and text
A proposed bill, not law, unless enacted; it lapses at the end of the session. In committee since January 26, 2026.
Pennsylvania House Bill 1459 (multiple-unit dwellings in commercial zones), bill page and text
A proposed bill, not law, unless enacted. Would reach only municipalities over 5,000 people in counties that grew between the last two censuses. In committee since May 13, 2025.
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit Qualified Census Tracts

A Qualified Census Tract lets a tax-credit project claim a 30% larger basis. Designations change every year; HUD's map item and layer text name different years (2026 and 2027), so the edition is stated as published. Being in a QCT does not mean a project will get credits.
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit Difficult Development Areas

In metro areas, Difficult Development Areas are ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs); outside them, whole counties. A tract is matched to ZCTAs by shared land area, so a tract on a ZCTA edge can be partly in a DDA.
Qualified Opportunity Zones designated for 2027 (second decennial round)

The new round of zones starts on 2027-01-01. The first-round zones (2018, on 2010 tracts) end on 2026-12-31 and are not shown. Treasury says taxpayers may not rely on the web list to support a tax position.
New Markets Tax Credit low-income community tracts (2016-2020 ACS)
U.S. Department of the Treasury, CDFI Fund

Shows whether a tract meets the poverty (20% or more) or income (80% of the benchmark or less) test. Other routes to eligibility (high-migration rural counties, targeted populations) are not shown. The CDFI Fund does not update the file every year.
National Register of Historic Places, listed property points and polygons
U.S. Department of the Interior, National Park Service

Only properties NPS has mapped and does not restrict are shown, so counts are a floor. A district polygon's homes are 2020 Census block homes whose block centre is inside it. Listing makes income-producing rehabilitation eligible for the federal historic tax credit; it does not grant one.
Keystone Opportunity Zone (KOZ) locations, public view
Pennsylvania Department of Community and Economic Development
Pennsylvania only. The sites DCED lists on its public KOZ map, with acreage and expiry year; it may not hold every active KOZ parcel. Contact names on the layer are not kept.
U.S. Department of Transportation, Bureau of Transportation Statistics

Stops as reported by agencies in their schedule feeds; some agencies are missing or out of date. Gives stop locations, not service frequency (frequency comes from the agency schedule feeds). About 673,000 stops nationally; queried by state bounding box in pages of at most 2,000.

Housing units and population are 2020 counts, not current. Internal points are a point inside each block, not its centre of population. Only the attribute table (the .dbf, about 46 MB of the 409 MB Pennsylvania zip) is read, by HTTP range requests; block shapes are never downloaded.
Philadelphia Water Department statement of citywide sewer service

A whole-city statement of the utility's service territory ("supplies drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater services to customers within the City of Philadelphia"; its wastewater page adds "combined sewers in approximately half of the city's neighborhoods and a separate sewer system in the other half"), not a parcel map: a few properties on private on-lot systems would not show. It says nothing about capacity for added homes or about combined-sewer overflow limits.
Montgomery County (PA) sewer service areas, July 2022 edition (via PASDA)
Montgomery County, Pennsylvania (Planning Commission); served by PASDA

A planning map of areas served by public sewer as of 2022; it does not show spare treatment or conveyance capacity, and a parcel inside an area may still need an extension. Homes outside every polygon are read as outside public sewer (the county inventory is treated as complete).
Adams County (PA) sewer service areas (existing), county GIS
Adams County, Pennsylvania (Office of Planning and Development GIS)
Approximate locations of public or community sewer from several authorities. The 17 "Future Sewer Service Area" polygons are left out; only the 36 existing areas count.
Pennsylvania public water supplier service areas (DEP, via PASDA)
Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection; served by PASDA

Present service-area boundaries of public water systems, made for the State Water Plan to find self-supplied areas; not a statement of spare supply. A home inside an area may still need a main extension.
EPA sewersheds of the United States (version 1.3) and their endpoint treatment plants
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Office of Research and Development, Office of Water)

Context only. Most boundaries are modelled with machine learning from hexagons of about 0.11 square km (Pennsylvania: 799 of 838 modelled; Vermont: 92 of 93 taken from a 2009 state map); EPA says they are not an authoritative source for property-level connections. Never used for a tract's sewer status.
Pennsylvania DEP Act 537 official plan status (plan age by municipality)

Gives only the date DEP last approved each municipality's official sewage facilities plan (or a pre-1971 county plan) and DEP's age class. An old plan is not a ban, and a recent plan is not spare capacity.
EPA Clean Watersheds Needs Survey 2022, documented needs by county
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Office of Water)

Capital needs states documented for the survey (projects eligible for Clean Water State Revolving Fund loans), summarized by county by EPA. Context only: a large need is not a shortage of capacity, and a zero can mean nothing was submitted.
FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (flood hazard zones and NFHL availability), public map service

The Special Flood Hazard Area is the regulatory 1% annual chance floodplain; it leaves out flooding from heavy rain away from mapped streams, and some maps are decades old. Where FEMA has no digital map (outside layer 0, "NFHL availability") flood shares are left blank rather than zero.
USGS Annual NLCD land cover and fractional impervious surface (Collection 1), MRLC coverage service
U.S. Geological Survey (Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium)
Satellite classification at 30 m: small lots, narrow streets and tree-covered yards are blurred; the developed classes include parks and lawns (class 21). Screening only.
USGS 3D Elevation Program bare-earth elevation (3DEPElevation image service)
Resampled by the service to 30 m (bilinear), so short steep banks are smoothed and the steep share is a lower bound for small sites. Screening only.
City of Philadelphia, Police Department (via OpenDataPhilly, Carto SQL)
One row per victim, police-involved shootings included. Location is the published block point. Records are revised after first publication. Philadelphia only.
Philadelphia Crime Incidents, Part I and II (Carto table incidents_part1_part2)

Incidents known to police, by the most serious offense (UCR general code); many offenses are never reported. Location is the hundred-block point. Not the FBI's agency counts, so not comparable with other places. Philadelphia only.
Philadelphia Licenses and Inspections Code Violations (Carto table violations)

Cases opened by inspectors, so they follow complaints and inspection effort as well as building condition. A 2020 record-system change and the 2020 pandemic lowered counts that year. Philadelphia only.

City of Philadelphia, Philly311 (via OpenDataPhilly, Carto SQL)
Requests show where residents call, not how much neglect there is. Request types were renamed over time (both names are counted). Philadelphia only.
City of Philadelphia, Office of Property Assessment (via OpenDataPhilly, Carto SQL)

Assessment records, not a census of who lives where. Market values are the City's mass-appraisal estimates. The last sale is the only sale on file, so repeat sales in a window are undercounted. Condominium units are filed as single family and are separated by building description.
City of Philadelphia, Department of Records (via OpenDataPhilly, Carto SQL)
Grantee names are judged entity or person by word list only. The single-family test uses today's property category, not the category on the sale date.

Philadelphia only. Large corporate investors are entities with 26 or more parcels; the share is of single-family rentals, not all homes.

Philadelphia only. Investors include named entities and individuals buying more than two homes; cash buyers are not counted, so it is a floor.

The top driver of each reform is worked out for the whole state, not for the district.

The binding factor is the funnel stage that loses the largest share of the step before it (assumptions/decision.yaml). The effect range is the paired difference, draw by draw, between a named variant (assumptions/variants.yaml) and the benchmark run of the same reform, on the same seed and draws.

Grade B: local and national data plus published studies; past ranges caught 54% of 1,004 back-test cases across this state's counties; local rules read for 12% of single-family lots; lot fit and legal share measured in Pennsylvania, take-up set by judgement; reform tested elsewhere (causal design).

Grade C: national data plus published studies; past ranges caught 54% of 1,004 back-test cases across this state's counties; fee pass-through and supply response set by judgement; law on record elsewhere, no measured result.

Grade C: national data plus published studies; past ranges caught 54% of 1,004 back-test cases across this state's counties; local rules read for 12% of single-family lots; single-family-only zoning share, lot fit and redevelopment rate set by judgement; reform tested elsewhere (causal design).

Grade C: national data plus published studies; past ranges caught 54% of 1,004 back-test cases across this state's counties; local rules read for 12% of residents; parking still built and cost pass-through set by judgement; reform tested elsewhere (matched comparison).

Grade C: multi-state and national data plus published studies; past ranges caught 54% of 1,004 back-test cases across this state's counties; local rules read for 12% of residents; developable land, redevelopment rate and net-new share set by judgement; results observed elsewhere (descriptive only).

A grade says how much evidence stands behind a number: source quality, the back-test, local law read, local or borrowed calibration, and outside evidence for the reform. It is not a probability and does not change any range.
